To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the male offspring of both diabetic parent had significantly higher insulin resistance, fasting insulin and leptin levels compared with those with one diabetic and non-diabetic parents.
male offspring of diabetic fathers have higher fasting glucose, insulin, HbA(1-c), C-peptide, 2h glucose, leptin, and HOMA-Insulin resistance than those with a diabetic father or a diabetic mother.
Male offspring of both diabetic (BDP) and one diabetic parent (BDP) had higher insulin resistance and fasting serum leptin levels than those with no diabetic parent (NDP).
In summary, our research is concerned with

the identification of risk factors for the development of T2DM in the male offspring of diabetic subjects, and the determination of whether these risk factors are influenced by the number of diabetic parents.
the influence of FH of T2DM on the metabolic profile of the male offspring of diabetic patients.
the identification of the genetic and metabolic factors that predispose to T2DM and its related metabolic abnormalities in young males with a history of T2DM in their family.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
male offspring of both diabetic (BDP) parents have higher insulin resistence and serum leptin and insulin levels compared to those of one diabetic parent (NDP) and offspring of non-diabetics (NDP).
the risk for T2DM in male offspring of BDP is higher than that in ODP, but lower than that in male offspring of non-diabetes mellitus parents.
the presence of a positive FH of T2DM in male offspring is associated with increased IR, hyperleptinemia and dyslipidemia, which are all well-established risk factors for T2DM.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
male offspring of BDP have higher insulin resistance (HOMA-IR) and serum leptin and triglyceride levels compared to ODP and NDP, respectively.
a positive family history of T2DM in offspring of diabetic parents is an important risk factor for the development of T2DM and its complications.
the male offspring of diabetic parent(s) are more insulin resistant and have higher leptin levels than those with non-diabetic parents.
The main takeaway from our work is that
male offspring of diabetic parent(s) should be carefully followed up and monitored for the presence of T2DM associated metabolic and endocrine risk factors, as well as for early signs of diabetes.

male offspring of both diabetic parent have higher insulin resistance, higher fasting and 2-hour serum insulin, higher serum triglycerides and higher leptin levels compared with those with one diabetic and non-diabetic parents.
the presence of a diabetic family history in both parents, especially in the father, increases the risk for T2DM in male offspring.
